My advice to getting started on a smaller scale, do a couple raised beds. The main advantage with raised beds is you don't have to worry about what kind of soil your land has, you just build a frame, and buy or create your own soil to put in it. You can even make a raised bed on solid rock, just make sure it is deep enough for the plants you want to grow. (Make sure you pick a short type of carrot for example)

A good place to start reading about raised beds: http://www.popularmechanics.com/home/lawn-garden/how-to/g92/build-raised-garden-beds/

For further reading, consider the square foot gardening method if you have limited space. I have had success loosely following his guidelines and I just like planting in concentrated blocks instead of long rows. His book was interesting, but their is plenty of info on various sites on the web if you don't feel like getting it. Libraries often carry older editions of it also.

http://squarefootgardening.org/square-foot-gardening-method

The most important aspect as I mentioned before was his spacing guidelines. This website has a good explanation.

http://www.mysquarefootgarden.net/plant-spacing/

Yes, bad form to reply to your own comment, but I thought of something else.

If you really want to a quick start without much work ahead of time, go buy bags of garden soil. Just arrange the bags in your yard where you may put raised beds later. The bags will help kill the grass underneath which is always good for gardening.

As to getting things growing, just cut holes in the bags and plant seeds/transplants. There you have it, almost instant garden, The soil will have enough food for the plants for a single season. Once garden season is done, and you have enjoyed your little taste of gardening, then build frames around the bags, and dump the soil out of the bags into your frame. Add a little more garden soil and compost, and boom, you have a raised bed ready to go for a fall garden.
